q: How do vision–language models process images?
short: A vision encoder splits the image into patches and embeds them; a projector maps these features into the LLM's embedding space; the resulting image tokens are interleaved with text tokens and processed by the same Transformer.
detail: Trained on image–text pairs, then instruction-tuned.
mistakes: Thinking images are converted to text captions first.

q: Image tokens for 336 × 336 with 14 × 14 patches?
short: 336/14 = 24 per side → 576 tokens.

q: How is audio tokenized?
short: Either as continuous encoder features per short frame (for understanding) or as discrete codes from a neural codec with several residual codebooks (for understanding and generation).
mistakes: Assuming audio uses the text tokenizer.

q: What enables million-token contexts?
short: Efficient exact attention kernels (FlashAttention), distributed sequence parallelism (Ring Attention), RoPE scaling with long-context training, smaller KV caches (GQA/MLA, quantization, paging), and sometimes sparse/hybrid attention.

q: What are reasoning models?
short: LLMs trained (often with RL on verifiable rewards) to produce long internal reasoning before answering, improving maths, code and planning; accuracy scales with thinking tokens.
mistakes: Equating them with CoT prompting only.

q: What does an integrated LLM product stack contain?
short: A base model, fine-tuning/alignment, prompts and structured output, retrieval, an agent loop with tools, guardrails, efficient serving, and evaluation/monitoring.
detail: Each layer must earn its place.

q: Why isn't a bigger model automatically safer?
short: Greater capability can enable more harmful uses, more convincing errors and more autonomous actions; safety depends on alignment, safeguards and evaluation that scale with capability, not on size.
mistakes: Assuming alignment improves automatically with scale.

q: 3 agent steps × 2,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens per step at $3/M in, $15/M out: cost?
Encoder features vs discrete codec tokens for audio?
short: Encoder features are rich and compact for understanding (ASR, QA) but not directly generable; codec tokens are discrete, enabling autoregressive speech generation and unified modelling, but are numerous (K codebooks × frame rate) and lossy.
mistakes: Assuming one approach fits all tasks.

q: How do models handle high-resolution images efficiently?
short: Tile the image into crops plus a low-resolution overview, pool or merge neighbouring patch tokens, use dynamic resolution, or compress with a learned resampler to a fixed number of tokens.
follow: Effect on reading small text in images?
mistakes: Feeding 3,000+ tokens per image by default.

q: How do you test long-context ability?
short: Needle-in-a-haystack retrieval at many positions and depths, multi-needle and reasoning-over-context tasks, long-document QA and summarisation, and comparison with RAG baselines; report performance by position.

q: What limits long-horizon agents today?
short: Compounding per-step errors, context management over hours, cost and latency, tool reliability, evaluation difficulty, and the need for oversight and permissions as actions become consequential.

q: Design a voice customer-service assistant.
short: Streaming speech encoder or ASR, LLM with RAG over policies and tools for account actions (with confirmations), guardrails and PII redaction, low-latency TTS or codec-token speech output, interruption handling, logging and evaluation of task success and latency.

q: KV cache at 128k tokens with GQA-8 (32 layers, head 128, 16-bit)?
mistakes: Using 4096 for KV width under GQA.

q: What do frontier safety evaluations test?
short: Dangerous capabilities (e.g. advanced cyber or bio assistance), autonomous replication or resource acquisition in agentic settings, deception and manipulation, and robustness of safeguards, alongside standard harm benchmarks and expert red teaming.

q: Plan an LLM product from scratch using the course.
short: Define tasks and evaluation set first (M14); try prompting with a strong model (M10–M11); add RAG for knowledge (M12); tools/agent only where needed (M13); fine-tune or distil for cost and style (M7); align and guard (M9, M15); optimise serving (M5–M6); monitor and iterate.

q: Unified any-to-any models: benefits and challenges?
short: One model reasons across modalities and can generate any of them, enabling natural voice and visual interaction; challenges: token budgets, balancing modality data, latency, evaluation across modalities, and new safety risks (e.g. voice impersonation, image misuse).

q: Long context or RAG for a 50,000-page knowledge base?
short: RAG: the corpus far exceeds any window, retrieval is cheaper and updatable, and permissions can be enforced; long context helps once relevant documents are retrieved (read whole sections). Combine them.

q: How does test-time compute change deployment economics?
short: Quality now scales with tokens spent per query, so cost becomes variable; systems route easy queries to fast paths and hard ones to long reasoning, set thinking budgets, and cache results, trading latency and cost for accuracy.
mistakes: Fixed maximum reasoning for every query.

q: What fundamentals remain constant across new advances?
short: Tokenization into sequences, attention and its memory costs, next-token training and scaling, decoding and serving bottlenecks, alignment trade-offs, retrieval for knowledge, and rigorous evaluation and safety, which apply equally to multimodal models and agents.
example: Image tokens still cost KV memory.
mistakes: Treating each new model type as entirely new.
